extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph), including how to weigh examples, predictability, examiner burdens, and applicant rebuttal. Focused on examination practice and office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) depends on whether one skilled in the art can make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the disclosure teaches how to make and use the invention in terms corresponding in scope to the claims; only an enabling disclosure is required, not demonstration of complete safety or all embodiments. The amount of required guidance depends on the nature of the invention, prior art, and predictability of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement when claim limited by a particular use
rubrics_metrics.description: When a compound or composition claim is limited by a particular use, enablement of that claim should be evaluated based on that limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim expressly recites a use, examiner should assess whether the specification enables that recited use (see In re Vaeck).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement when claim not limited by a recited use / multiple disclosed uses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a compound/composition claim is not limited by a recited use, any enabled use that reasonably correlates with the entire scope of the claim is sufficient to preclude an enablement rejection. If multiple uses are disclosed, an enablement rejection must explain why the specification fails to enable each disclosed use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any disclosed use is enabled when multiple uses are present, the application is enabling for the claimed invention; a rejection must be supported with explanations and evidence as to lack of enablement for each use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working vs. prophetic examples
rubrics_metrics.description: An example may be 'working' (based on work actually performed) or 'prophetic' (describing predicted results rather than work actually conducted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims/specification should assist readers in differentiating working and prophetic examples (prophetic examples should use future or present tense rather than past). The presence or absence of examples does not by itself determine enablement; prophetic examples are not per se non-enabling, but must not be misrepresented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of absence of working examples / single working example
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of working examples or lack of evidence that the claimed invention works should never be the sole reason for rejecting claims for nonenablement; a single working example can preclude a rejection that 'nothing is enabled.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a single working example may prevent a blanket non-enablement rejection, it should not automatically allow broad claim scope without analysis — examiner must evaluate whether extrapolation from that example to the full claimed scope would require undue experimentation and must explain why extrapolation is or is not reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between in vitro/in vivo examples and claimed method
rubrics_metrics.description: An in vitro or in vivo animal model example constitutes a 'working example' only if that example 'correlates' with a disclosed or claimed method of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlation depends on state of the prior art; examiner must give reasons for concluding lack of correlation and weigh evidence for and against correlation. A rigorous exact correlation is not required; reasonable correlation based on probative evidence may suffice (see In re Brana, Cross v. Iizuka).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative examples for a claimed genus
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claimed genus, representative examples together with a statement applicable to the genus as a whole will ordinarily be sufficient if one skilled in the art would expect the claimed genus could be used without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of enablement for other members of the genus is required only where the examiner advances adequate reasons showing a skilled person could not use the genus as a whole without undue experimentation. Sometimes a few examples plus a general quality 'running through' the class can suffice (Amgen v. Sanofi citing Incandescent Lamp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic examples mischaracterized as actual
rubrics_metrics.description: When prophetic examples are described ambiguously or in a way that implies results are actual, the adequacy and accuracy of the disclosure may be called into question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If so, examiners should consider rejection under enablement and/or written description; applicants should reply with actual test results or persuasive arguments/declarations (without introducing new matter). Misrepresenting prophetic examples in past tense can raise inequitable conduct concerns (Hoffmann‑La Roche v. Promega; Apotex v. UCB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability of the art affects required enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of guidance or direction needed to enable the invention is inversely related to what is known in the prior art and to predictability in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In predictable arts (mechanical/electrical), a single species may provide broad enablement; in unpredictable arts (chemical, physiological), more disclosure may be required. Nascent technology requires a 'specific and useful teaching.' Courts/cases (Chiron, Marzocchi, Fisher) illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's initial burden to question enablement and claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Before analyzing enablement, the examiner must construe the claims and, for unclear terms, select and state the intended definition and scope in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make a rejection, examiner has initial burden to establish a reasonable basis to question enablement and must give reasons explaining the uncertainty; must back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning and provide specific technical reasons (In re Wright, In re Marzocchi, Genentech v. Wellcome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of all enablement factors and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An enablement analysis must consider all relevant factors and evidence; it is improper to conclude nonenablement based on analysis of only one factor while ignoring others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should make specific fact findings supported by evidence and draw conclusions from those facts (Wands). The examiner must identify missing information and explain why it cannot be supplied without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution / presenting best rejection early
rubrics_metrics.description: Under compact prosecution principles, the first Office action on the merits should present the best case with all relevant reasons, issues, and evidence for an enablement rejection so applicant can rebut and so subsequent actions may be made final where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner recognizes claim limitations that would render claims enabled, those should be communicated to applicant as early as possible so enabled, allowable subject matter is identified promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of enablement based on the evidence as a whole; applicant's burden to rebut
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examiner establishes a reasonable basis to question enablement, burden shifts to applicant to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the application as a guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may submit 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations or cite references; evidence need only be convincing by a preponderance standard. Examiner must compare any post‑filing declarations' experimental steps to the specification to ensure commensurate scope and then weigh all evidence without relying on personal opinion (In re Brandstadter, In re Buchner, Pac. Biosciences v. Oxford Nanopore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be enabling as of the filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is judged as of the filing date based on the nature of the invention, the state of the prior art at filing, and the level of skill in the art at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State of the art at filing determines how much direction is needed; later publications generally cannot be used to supplement the disclosure though they may be evidence of what skilled artisans knew (exceptions where later work shows impossibility at filing). Examiner generally should not rely on post‑filing references to show nonenablement except in narrow circumstances (Chiron, In re Wright).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable persons skilled in the relevant art(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable persons skilled in the art to which the invention pertains; where different arts are involved, it must enable persons skilled in each art to carry out the aspect applicable to their specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pertinent art should be defined by the problem to be solved. Disclosure need not repeat what is well-known. Multi‑disciplinary inventions may require disclosures enabling specialists in each field to cooperate to practice the invention (Technicon v. Alpkem; Ex parte Zechnall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity and quality of experimentation (undue experimentation / Wands factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of experimentation needed to practice the invention is one factor (undue experimentation) but reasonableness depends on nature of the invention and underlying art; extensive routine experimentation may be permissible if sufficient direction is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time and expense are factors but not controlling; difficulty and complexity of assays or of components may make experimentation undue in some arts (examples: Telectronics — held reasonable despite time/cost; Amgen — lack of enablement where claim scope required screening millions of candidates). The specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation; quantity of examples is only one factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify missing information for enablement rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If enablement doubt arises because information is missing about one or more essential claim elements or relationships between parts, the examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and why it is needed to provide enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should state which essential information is lacking and explain why a skilled artisan could not develop that information without undue experimentation; references should be supplied if possible to support a prima facie case (MPEP § 2164.06(a)).
